catalog_quote: The first important feature to remark is that stress is non-phonemic, just as in the other Campan languages. ... there are certain patterns; yet they cannot be formulated in terms of rules, but rather in terms of tendencies, i.e. there are stress patterns that are not rigidly applied and can be violated, so that a word may have the tendency to have the stress in a given position, but this position can change without sounding strange to a speaker. ... in bi- and trisyllabic words, the stress is on the penultimate, and, in tetrasyllabic words, it is on the antepenultimate ... the last syllable is extrametrical and the stress falls on the second syllable of each disyllabic foot ... Exceptions to this regular pattern are caused in the first place by the existence of bimoraic syllables, which appear to be the strongest stress attractor. sweep_summary: One title-hit only: Spring 1990 'How many feet per language' (WCCFL 9, pp.493-508). It is a prosodic-morphology paper on Axininca Campa, i.e. Payne 1981's Apurucayali dialect (Glottolog ajyi1238/cpc), not Ashéninka Pajonal; Glottolog's cjo filing stems from Fabre's lumped 'Asheninka y Campa del Pajonal' list. Verified from McCarthy & Prince 1993 (ROA-482, open; cites Spring 1990b:501 on Minimal Word / PrWd base in Axininca and gives the full bibliographic entry), Wikipedia's Axininca bibliography, Open Library / archive.org records, and the scanned preface of Payne 1981 (SIL scan via Wayback; data from Puerto Davis on the Apurucayali). No open copy of Spring 1990 exists (no DOI; print CSLI volume; archive.org scan is lending-restricted), so it is unread, relevance other-language-or-variety, priority none for this language. Nothing in this sweep bears on the catalog's weight-hedged coding for ashe1273; Pedrós 2023 remains the sole and deciding stress description. Files ( updated). Note for the parent: the McCarthy & Prince appendix (pp.159-163) is an open secondary summary of Apurucayali iambic stress with final stresslessness, based on Payne, Payne & Santos 1982:185-195, should an ajyi1238 record ever be wanted (none exists in the store).

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote: confirmed verbatim in the held Pedrós 2023 text at Section 2.5, pp.81 and 83, with the heavy-syllable statements at pp.84 and 90; locator correct. (2) Deciding source: a 2023 701-pp reference grammar with a dedicated stress section; nothing better exists for this variety (no phonology article, no instrumental work; Heitzman's SIL output on Pajonal Campa is lexical-comparative and discourse; the 2018 Nopoki guide is pedagogical). The 'weight-hedged' / QS-HEDGED coding faithfully reflects the source: iambic L-to-R with final extrametricality as default, (C)VV the strongest attractor even word-finally, (C)VN not heavy, all framed by the author as non-rigid tendencies; the 13/20 rule-fit noted in contra[1] is what the author himself predicts. sources.citation: Glottolog reference search: author=Heitzman; title contains 'pajonal' (25 hits)
sources.quote: No phonology/stress work on Pajonal Ashéninka is listed: Heitzman 1973/1975 (Proto-Campa consonant correspondences, cognate sets), Heitzman & Shaler 1979 (texts/concordance), Heitzman 1981/1991/1992 (narrative discourse), Shaler 1985 (music), plus ethnography; the only grammar is Pedrós 2023.

sources.citation: WALS Online, language 'Campa Pajonal Asheninca' (wals code cpa), valuesets 14A/15A/16A (Goedemans & van der Hulst)
sources.quote: 14A 'No fixed stress', 15A 'Not predictable', 16A 'No weight', all referenced solely to Pike & Kindberg 1956 'A problem in multiple stresses' (Word 12). Kindberg's 'Campa' is Tambo-Ene Asháninka, not Pajonal/Ucayali Ashéninka, so the StressTyp2/WALS 'NMS' coding listed in our record's contra[0] is a database attribution to the wrong Ashé-Ashá variety rather than an independent description of this language.
